newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris sought youth smoking data - report.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris sought youth smoking data - report.

text.p: Internal company documents show that Philip Morris Cos Inc used pollsters in the 1970s to quiz youngsters about their smoking habits at drive-ins, bowling alleys and beaches, a newspaper reported Sunday.

Studies conducted between 1970 and 1988 by research and marketing experts at Philip Morris show how the largest U.S. tobacco company, which denies ever targeting children, looked for information about the smoking and buying habits of the nation's youth, the Richmond Times-Dispatch reported.
Company documents were given to the Times-Dispatch by plaintiffs' lawyers who are suing the tobacco industry, the newspaper said.

A June 12, 1970, memo to Philip Morris from Roper Researchers Associates of New York said: "True answers on smoking habits might be difficult to elicit in the presence of parents," the newspaper reported.
"We recommend interviewing young people at summer recreation centers (at beaches, public pools, lakes, etc.)," the memo said, adding that the target group was as young as 14 years of age.
Anti-smoking activists contend the studies support their charge that Philip Morris and other tobacco companies have spent decades styding the youth smoking market, the Times-Dispatch said.
Company officials denied the charge and said the leaking of internal memos was part of a lobbying effort to pressure the industry to settle about 240 lawsuits, the paper said.
Michael York, an attorney representing Philip Morris, said the documents showed media manipulation, the newspaper said.
"There's a phalanx of entreprenurial plaintiffs' lawyers making charges that simply can't be supported by the facts," York told the Times-Dispatch.
He dismissed the polling studies as old material released by anti-tobacco lawyers "to influence judges and potential jurors" around the country.

The newspaper said that while the papers do not prove that Philip Morris lured children to smoke, they do show that youth market issues were discussed with high-level executives. Among the officials on the memos' distribution list were Clifford Goldsmith, who ran the company's global operations, and Frank Resnick, a top research official, the newspaper said.

In addition to the 1970 memo from the Roper group that pointed out the need to survey 14- to 17-year-olds away from home to get "true answers," a report from Philip Morris' Marketing Research Department indicated company pollsters carried out a plan to interview children, the paper said.
"Young smokers were sought out in 35 locations around the country at popular 'hangouts,' at drive-ins, bowling alleys, near military bases, at beaches, etc.," a July 25, 1974, report said.
